'''Decipher after the Star Wars license''' covers [[Decipher]], Inc. after its ''Star Wars'' license ended on 31 December 2001. Decipher kept publishing ''The Lord of the Rings'' and ''Star Trek'' card games until 2007 and launched role-playing games and an original-IP card game. Layoffs and an embezzlement case weakened the company.

== The Star Wars games wind down (2001–2002) ==

Decipher announced on 28 December 2001 that Lucasfilm had not extended its license.<ref name="ann122801" /> The trading-card rights went to Wizards of the Coast, which planned a new ''Star Wars'' card game with ''Episode II'' content for 2002.<ref name="icv2-2002" /> The license loss ended all three of Decipher's ''Star Wars'' games: SWCCG, the ''Young Jedi'' CCG and the ''Jedi Knights'' TCG.<ref name="wp-decipher" />

SWCCG's last expansion, [[Theed Palace]], shipped in December 2001.<ref name="encyc3" /> ''Young Jedi'''s last set, ''Boonta Eve Podrace'', was released on 5 September 2001,<ref name="wp-yj" /> and ''Jedi Knights'' had its second expansion in October 2001.<ref name="wp-jk" /> Remaining SWCCG product was sold off at heavy discounts.<ref name="encyc3" /> Some of it was later repacked by third parties; see [[Unofficial repackaged products]].

In early 2002 Decipher set up the volunteer [[Players Committee]] to run SWCCG tournaments and rulings.<ref name="pc1" /> It donated over one million dollars in product, promotional material and financial backing to it.<ref name="tfn-donation" /><ref name="encyc3" /> See [[History of the Players Committee]].

== The Lord of the Rings and Star Trek (2001–2007) ==

Decipher had acquired the card-game license for New Line Cinema's ''The Lord of the Rings'' films in 2001, which became its main line once ''Star Wars'' was gone.<ref name="wp-decipher" /> ''The Lord of the Rings'' TCG won the 2001 Origins Award for best trading card game.<ref name="origins2001" /> In 2002 Decipher relaunched the ''Star Trek'' CCG as Second Edition, first released on 12 December 2002.<ref name="wp-stccg" />

Both lines ended in 2007, when Decipher's licenses expired. ''The Lord of the Rings'' TCG closed with its final expansion, ''Age's End''.<ref name="lotr-end" /> On 12 December 2007 Decipher announced that the ''Star Trek'' CCG would end with the expansion ''What You Leave Behind''.<ref name="st-end" />

== Role-playing games (2002–2005) ==

In 2002 Decipher acquired most of the studio of Last Unicorn Games and published ''Star Trek'' and ''The Lord of the Rings'' role-playing games on its own CODA system.<ref name="wp-decipher" /><ref name="tdm2003" /> ''The Lord of the Rings Roleplaying Game'' won the 2002 Origins Award for best role-playing game.<ref name="origins2002" /> Decipher shut down its RPG lines around 2005.<ref name="wp-decipher" />

== Youth licenses and WARS (2003–2005) ==

Decipher tried the younger market again with ''.hack//Enemy'' (2003; 2003 Origins Award for best trading card game),<ref name="origins2003" /> ''Beyblade'' (2003) and ''Mega Man NT Warrior'' (2004).<ref name="wp-decipher" />

The ''WARS'' Trading Card Game, released in October 2004, was Decipher's only card game on its own intellectual property. It used rules adapted from SWCCG, with backstory by Michael A. Stackpole. After two releases it was put "on hiatus" in May 2005.<ref name="wp-wars" /> In 2005 Decipher also cancelled ''.hack'' and ''Mega Man'' and laid off up to 40 employees.<ref name="wp-decipher" /><ref name="waterside" />

== Embezzlement case ==

In March 2009 Rick Eddleman, Decipher's vice president of finance since 1993 and Warren Holland's brother-in-law, pleaded guilty to embezzling more than $1.5 million from the company from 2000 onward.<ref name="pilot2009a" /> He was sentenced on 27 July 2009 to six years and five months in prison.<ref name="pilot2009b" />

== Fight Klub and later years (2008–) ==

In late 2007 Decipher replaced its home page with a teaser promising "a player revolution" in 2008.<ref name="reinvent" /> In March 2008 it began recruiting founding members for ''Fight Klub'',<ref name="fk2008" /> a card game built on several action-film licenses, released in February 2009.<ref name="wp-decipher" /> In January 2012 Decipher's site announced it would also host ''How to Host a Murder'' material.<ref name="htham2012" />

Decipher's ''WARS'' setting continued in fiction: Grail Quest Books published two novels, and from 2021 Arcbeatle Press reprinted and completed the trilogy as ''WARSONG''.<ref name="goshen2022" />
